title: In a fertility advance, engineered molecular glue stabilizes chromosomes in aging eggs
summary: Researchers engineered a protein system capable of restoring normal chromosome connections in aging mouse eggs, raising hopes of one day improving IVF outcomes
content: Around the world, people are increasingly choosing to have babies later in life for reasons both social and economic. As they get older though, they face a mounting biological challenge: genetic errors caused by chromosomes failing to separate correctly. This phenomenon, known as aneuploidy, is the leading cause of age-related infertility, failed in-vitro fertilization (IVF) cycles, and miscarriage, and it increases dramatically around the age of 40. Studies have shown that between 50% and 80% of embryos from women in their 40s carry chromosomal abnormalities. One of the main drivers of aneuploidy is the loss of a protein complex called cohesin, which acts like a molecular glue holding chromosomes together. In a new study, researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen, Germany, engineered a novel protein system capable of restoring normal chromosome connections in aging mouse eggs. The study, published Thursday in Science , raises the possibility of one day developing such a system into a treatment that could reduce aneuploidy in human eggs used for IVF. Read the rest…

title: STAT+: The grueling struggle to find a primary care doctor in the ‘medical capital’ of America
summary: Boston is supposed to be the medical capital of America. Yet many don’t have primary care access, hurting their ability to get treatments, screenings, and medical advice.
content: I was three days into calling doctors’ offices, trying to get a primary care appointment. Over and over, I sat on hold, only to hear I’d have to wait weeks or months. It was mind numbing. Then I reached a voicemail greeting that sounded about as despondent as I felt. “We’ve received an extremely high volume of messages due to multiple providers in our area retiring or leaving their practice very recently,” the woman’s voice said with a hint of exasperation, “so please understand it may take longer than normal to receive a return call back.” Continue to STAT+ to read the full story…
authors: Marin Wolf, Jonathan Saltzman,and and Scooty Nickerson — Boston Globe
